questionMarkdown:
Evaluate the following expression by repeated squaring method. Show the steps.

$$8^{1027}\bmod22$$
independentVerification: Independently squared to i=10: residues8,20,4,16,14,20,4,16,14,20,4; selected2^10+2+1 gives4*20*8 mod22=2. No coprimality needed.
officialMarkdown:
Source: [physical PDF page 14](../sources/papers/2019-midterm.pdf#page=14).

By the repeated squaring method, we have
$$\begin{aligned}8^{2^0}&\equiv8\pmod{22}\\8^{2^1}&\equiv8^2\equiv20\pmod{22}\\8^{2^2}&\equiv20^2\equiv4\pmod{22}\\8^{2^3}&\equiv4^2\equiv16\pmod{22}\\8^{2^4}&\equiv16^2\equiv14\pmod{22}\\8^{2^5}&\equiv14^2\equiv20\pmod{22}.\end{aligned}$$
We have $1027=2^0+2^1+2^{10}$.
$8^{2^{10}}\equiv4\pmod{22}$ since $8^{2^i}\equiv4\pmod{22}$ if $i\equiv2\pmod4$.
$$\begin{aligned}8^{1027}&\equiv8^{2^0+2^1+2^{10}}\pmod{22}\\&\equiv8^{2^0}\cdot8^{2^1}\cdot8^{2^{10}}\pmod{22}\\&\equiv8\cdot20\cdot4\pmod{22}\\&\equiv2\pmod{22}.\end{aligned}$$
Therefore, we have $8^{1027}\bmod22=2$.
solutionMarkdown:
**Answer.** $2$.

**Derivation/proof.** The residues for $8^{2^i}$ at $i=0,1,\ldots,10$ are $8,20,4,16,14,20,4,16,14,20,4$, obtained each time by squaring the previous residue modulo 22. For example $8^2\equiv20$, $20^2\equiv4$, $4^2\equiv16$, $16^2\equiv14$, $14^2\equiv20$. Since $1027=2^{10}+2^1+2^0$, multiply the selected residues: $4\cdot20\cdot8=640\equiv2\pmod{22}$. Direct modular exponentiation independently gives 2.

The full table for $i=0,1,\ldots,10$ is $8,20,4,16,14,20,4,16,14,20,4$. The final product is $640=29\cdot22+2$. Repeated squaring works despite $\gcd(8,22)\ne1$.

independentVerification: 1161=1024+128+8+1. Independent square table6,36,92,36,92,36,92,36,92,36,92; selected product gives216 mod602. Noncoprime base valid for repeated squaring.
officialMarkdown:
Source: [PDF physical page 8](../sources/papers/2016-final.pdf#page=8).

(a)
$$\lfloor\log_2 1161\rfloor=10$$
$$\begin{aligned}
R_1&=6^2\bmod602=6\times6\bmod602=36\\
R_2&=6^4\bmod602=R_1\times R_1\bmod602=92\\
R_3&=6^8\bmod602=R_2\times R_2\bmod602=36\\
R_4&=6^{16}\bmod602=R_3\times R_3\bmod602=92\\
R_5&=6^{32}\bmod602=R_4\times R_4\bmod602=36\\
R_6&=6^{64}\bmod602=R_5\times R_5\bmod602=92\\
R_7&=6^{128}\bmod602=R_6\times R_6\bmod602=36\\
R_8&=6^{256}\bmod602=R_7\times R_7\bmod602=92\\
R_9&=6^{512}\bmod602=R_8\times R_8\bmod602=36\\
R_{10}&=6^{1024}\bmod602=R_9\times R_9\bmod602=92
\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}
6^{1161}\bmod602&=6^{1024+128+8+1}\bmod602\\&=6^{1024}\cdot6^{128}\cdot6^8\cdot6^1\bmod602\\&=92\cdot36\cdot36\cdot6\bmod602\\&=216
\end{aligned}$$
solutionMarkdown:
**Answer.** $216$.

**Derivation/proof.** Since $6^2\equiv36$, $6^4\equiv36^2\equiv92$, and $6^8\equiv92^2\equiv36\pmod{602}$, successive squarings alternate 36 and 92. As $1161=1024+128+8+1$, $6^{1161}\equiv92\cdot36\cdot36\cdot6\pmod{602}$. Reducing the products gives $92\cdot36\equiv302$, $302\cdot36\equiv36$, then $36\cdot6=216$.

independentVerification: 17 mod14=3;3^3=-1 mod14;2023=674*3+1 and674 is even, so remainder3. Independent modular pow gives3.
officialMarkdown:
Source: [physical PDF page 10](../sources/papers/COMP2711_F2023_Final.pdf#page=10).

> (b) $17\equiv3\pmod{14}$ So we have: $3^3\equiv27\equiv-1\pmod{14}$. $(3^3)^{674}\equiv3^{2022}\equiv(-1)^{674}\equiv1\pmod{14}$ $3^{2023}\equiv3\cdot3^{2022}\equiv3\cdot1\equiv3$.
solutionMarkdown:
**Answer.** $3$.

**Derivation/proof.** Since $17\equiv3\pmod{14}$ and $3^3=27\equiv-1\pmod{14}$, write $2023=3\cdot674+1$. Then
$$17^{2023}\equiv3^{2023}=(3^3)^{674}\cdot3\equiv(-1)^{674}\cdot3=3\pmod{14}.$$
The residue 3 is already between 0 and 13, so it is the requested remainder. Equivalently, $3^6\equiv1$ and $2023\equiv1\pmod6$, confirming the same cycle calculation.

Because $2023=3\cdot674+1$, the remaining expression is $(-1)^{674}\cdot3=3$. This is already in the standard remainder range $0\le r<14$.

independentVerification: 109 prime (trial divisors2,3,5,7). 542=5*108+2; base2 nonzero, FLT yields4. Independent pow gives4.
officialMarkdown:
Source: [physical PDF page 3](../sources/papers/2022-midterm.pdf#page=3).

> (a) 109 is a prime number. By using Fermat's Little Theorem: $2^{108}\equiv1\pmod{109}\implies(2^{108})^5\equiv1^5\implies2^{540}\equiv1\pmod{109}$. So $2^{542}=2^2\cdot2^{540}\equiv2^2\equiv4\pmod{109}$.
solutionMarkdown:
**Answer.** $4$.

**Derivation/proof.** 109 is prime and 2 is coprime to it, so 2^108≡1 mod 109. Divide the exponent: 542=5·108+2. Then 2^542=(2^108)^5·2²≡1·4≡4 mod 109. The representative4 already lies between0 and 108.

Specifically $542=5\cdot108+2$ and $2^{542}=(2^{108})^5\cdot2^2$.

independentVerification: 47 mod11=3;FLT period10. Exponent37^27 mod10 independently equals3 via7^4=1 and27 mod4=3;final3^3 mod11=5. Nested exponent reduced under different modulus.
officialMarkdown:
Source: [physical PDF page 10](../sources/papers/COMP2711_S2025_Midterm.pdf#page=10).

(b) $47\equiv3\pmod{11}$. We also know that $3^{10}\equiv1\pmod{11}$ (based on little Fermat theorem).

We need to calculate $37^{27}\pmod{10}$.
$$37^{27}\equiv7^{27}\equiv7\cdot7^{26}\equiv7\cdot49^{13}\equiv7\cdot9^{13}\equiv7\cdot9\equiv63\equiv3\pmod{10}$$
$$3^{37^{27}}\equiv3^{10k+3}\equiv27\cdot(3^{10})^k\equiv27\equiv5\pmod{11}$$
solutionMarkdown:
**Answer.** $5$.

**Derivation/proof.** The prime 11 is coprime to 3, so Fermat's Little Theorem gives $3^{10}\equiv1\pmod{11}$. Since $47\equiv3\pmod{11}$, compute $37^{27}\bmod10$ separately. Modulo ten, $37\equiv7$, $7^2\equiv9$ and $7^4\equiv1$, hence $7^{27}=(7^4)^6\cdot7^3\equiv343\equiv3\pmod{10}$. Write $37^{27}=10k+3$. Therefore $47^{37^{27}}\equiv3^{10k+3}\equiv(3^{10})^k3^3\equiv27\equiv5\pmod{11}$. The intermediate residue three belongs to the exponent; the final residue five belongs to the entire power.

questionMarkdown:
Let $p\ge7$ be a prime. Prove that the number with decimal representation
$$\underbrace{1111\cdots1}_{\text{p-1 times}}$$
is divisible by $p$.
Note: For example, in the special case $p=7$, note that 111111 is divisible by 7, since $111111=7\times15873$.
Hint 1: Express the number as the sum of powers of 10.
Hint 2: You may find Fermat’s Little Theorem helpful.
independentVerification: For prime p>=7, p divides neither10 nor9. Telescoping9*(1+10+...+10^(p-2))=10^(p-1)-1 and FLT imply9S=0 modp;inverse9 givesS=0. Checked representative primes7..199 with modular summation; proof covers all.
officialMarkdown:
Source: [physical PDF page 16](../sources/papers/COMP2711_S2024_Midterm.pdf#page=16), [physical PDF page 17](../sources/papers/COMP2711_S2024_Midterm.pdf#page=17).

> Answer.
> Call the given number $S$. We want to prove that $p\mid S$. Following Hint 1, note that $S$ can be written as: $S=10^0+10^1\cdots+10^{p-2}$.
> This is the sum of the first $p-1$ terms of a geometric series, for which we can apply the formula: $r^0+r^1\cdots+r^{n-1}=\frac{r^n-1}{r-1}$, where $r\ne1$. Substituting $r:=10,n:=p-1$, we obtain:
> $$S=10^0+10^1\ldots10^{p-2}=\frac{10^{p-1}-1}{10-1}=\frac{10^{p-1}-1}9.$$
> Rearranging, we get that: $9S=10^{p-1}-1$.
> Taking this equation mod $p$, we get: $9S\equiv10^{p-1}-1\pmod p$. (*)
> Since $p$ is a prime greater than or equal to 7, it follows that $p$ and 10 have no common factors. Following Hint 2, we note that Fermat's Little Theorem is applicable here, and we can use it to obtain $10^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p$. (**)
> Substituting from (??) into (??), we get: $9S\equiv10^{p-1}-1\equiv1-1\equiv0\pmod p$, which implies that $p\mid9S$.
> Since $p$ is a prime and $p\mid9S$, it follows that either $p\mid9$ or $p\mid S$, but since $9=3\cdot3$ and $p\ge7$, it cannot be the case that $p\mid9$. Therefore, we conclude that $p\mid S$.
solutionMarkdown:
**Answer.** $p$ divides the repunit with $p-1$ digits.

**Derivation/proof.** Let $S=1+10+\cdots+10^{p-2}$, with $p-1$ terms. Geometric summation gives $9S=10^{p-1}-1$. Since $p\ge7$ is prime, $p\nmid10$, and Fermat's Little Theorem gives $10^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p$. Thus $9S\equiv0\pmod p$. Also $p\nmid9$, so the prime product property implies $p\mid S$ from $p\mid9S$. The two exclusions respectively justify applying Fermat and cancelling nine, completing the proof.

questionMarkdown: Alice and Bob share a key using the Diffie-Hellman key exchange algorithm with $a=17,p=31,k_1=34$ and $k_2=41$. What is the shared key? Note that the shared key must be in $\mathbb Z_p$. Use Fermat’s Little Theorem and the repeated squaring method to simplify the calculation. Show all the computational steps.
independentVerification: 31 prime;34*41=1394=46*30+14.17^2,17^4,17^8 mod31=10,7,18;product1260 mod31=20. Independent two-party calculations both20.
officialMarkdown:
Source: [physical PDF page 2](../sources/papers/2021-midterm.pdf#page=2).

> The shared key is $a^{k_1k_2}\bmod p=17^{34\cdot41}\bmod31$.
>
> By Fermat's Little Theorem, $17^{34\cdot41}\equiv17^{34\cdot41\bmod30}\equiv17^{4\cdot11\bmod30}\equiv17^{14}\pmod{31}$.
>
> We compute the shared key by repeated squaring method.
>
> $$\begin{aligned}
> 17^{2^1}\bmod31&=10\\
> 17^{2^2}\bmod31&=10^2\bmod31=7\\
> 17^{2^3}\bmod31&=7^2\bmod31=18
> \end{aligned}$$
>
> Note that $17^{14}=17^{2^1+2^2+2^3}$. So,
>
> $$\begin{aligned}
> 17^{14}&\equiv17^{2^1}17^{2^2}17^{2^3}\\
> &\equiv10\cdot7\cdot18\\
> &\equiv20\pmod{31}.
> \end{aligned}$$
solutionMarkdown:
**Answer.** $20$.

**Derivation/proof.** Both parties obtain $a^{k_1k_2}\bmod p$, here $17^{1394}\bmod31$. Since 31 is prime and 17 is nonzero modulo 31, Fermat gives period 30; 1394≡14 mod 30. Repeated squaring gives $17^2\equiv289\equiv10$, $17^4\equiv10^2\equiv7$, $17^8\equiv7^2\equiv18$ modulo 31. As 14=8+4+2, multiply $18\cdot7\cdot10=1260\equiv20$. This lies in the required residue range 0,…,30.

Explicitly, $1394=46\cdot30+14$ and $17^{30}\equiv1\pmod{31}$. The base is coprime to the prime modulus, which is essential for Fermat reduction.

The final square and reduction are $17^8\equiv49\equiv18$ and $1260\equiv20\pmod{31}$.

questionMarkdown:
Consider Bob is using RSA algorithm for public key cryptography. Bob starts by picking the two prime numbers $p=43$ and $q=23$. So, $n=pq=989$.

(c) Suppose Bob’s public key is $(989,53)$ and Alice wants to send a message $m=720$ to Bob. Write down the modular expression that computes the encrypted message $c$. It is not necessary to evaluate the expression.
independentVerification: Substitute message720<n989 and public exponent53 in encryption C=m^e modn. No private exponent required. Original shared context preserved.
officialMarkdown:
Source: [physical PDF page 13](../sources/papers/2019-midterm.pdf#page=13).

The encrypted message $c=720^{53}\bmod989$.
solutionMarkdown:
**Answer.** $c=720^{53}\bmod989$.

**Derivation/proof.** RSA encryption maps a message representative $m$ to $m^e\bmod n$, using the recipient's public key. Substitute $m=720,e=53,n=989$. The message is already in $\mathbb Z_{989}$, so the expression is valid without first reducing it. The private exponent is not used for this encryption request.

The private decryption exponent $401$ must not replace the public exponent $53$.

questionMarkdown: We implement a “toy example” of the RSA cryptosystem by choosing two prime numbers $p=23$ and $q=37$. Assume that we use $(851,17)$ as the public key in this example. Compute the private decryption key. Show all your calculations.
independentVerification: 23 and37 prime, n851 andT792. Extended Euclid yields233*17-5*792=1. Inverse233 checked directly; all x=0..850 round-trip using e17,d233 including nonunits.
officialMarkdown:
Source: [physical PDF page 13](../sources/papers/COMP2711_S2024_Midterm.pdf#page=13).

> Answer. $n=p\cdot q=23\times37=851$, $e=17$.
> $t=\phi(n)=(p-1)(q-1)=(23-1)\times(37-1)=792$.
> The private key $d$ satisfies $e\cdot d\equiv1\pmod t$, which means $d=(17)^{-1}\pmod{792}$.
> Using the extended Euclidean algorithm.
> $$\begin{array}{lll}\gcd(792,17)&792=46\times17+10&10=792-46\times17\quad(1)\\\gcd(17,10)&17=1\times10+7&7=17-1\times10\quad(2)\\\gcd(10,7)&10=1\times7+3&3=10-1\times7\quad(3)\\\gcd(7,3)&7=2\times3+1&1=7-2\times3\quad(4)\end{array}$$
> Substituting:
> $$\begin{aligned}1&=7-2\times3&&\text{(By (4))}\\&=7-2\times(10-1\times7)&&\text{(By (3))}\\&=(-2)\times10+3\times7\\&=(-2)\times10+3\times(17-1\times10)&&\text{(By (2))}\\&=3\times17+(-5)\times10\\&=3\times17+(-5)\times(792-46\times17)&&\text{(By (1))}\\&=(-5)\times792+233\times17.\end{aligned}$$
> Therefore, the private key $d=233$.
> Remark: $d$ must be a positive number. Considering that we are using $C^d\bmod n$ to compute the original message $M$, it is necessary to compute a positive multiplicative inverse.
solutionMarkdown:
**Answer.** $d=233$; the private key may be written $(851,233)$.

**Derivation/proof.** $n=23\cdot37=851$ and $\varphi(n)=22\cdot36=792$. Solve $17d\equiv1\pmod{792}$. The Euclidean divisions are $792=46\cdot17+10$, $17=10+7$, $10=7+3$, and $7=2\cdot3+1$. Back-substitution gives $1=7-2(10-7)=3\cdot7-2\cdot10=3\cdot17-5\cdot10=233\cdot17-5\cdot792$. Hence $d\equiv233\pmod{792}$ and we choose the positive representative $233$. Directly, $17\cdot233=3961=5\cdot792+1$, confirming the inverse.

questionMarkdown:
This problem is on the RSA algorithm for public key cryptogtaphy. To generate his keys, Bob uses two prime numbers $p=7,q=11$. So, $n=pq=77$ and $T=(p-1)(q-1)=60$.

(iii) [3 pts] Suppose Alice wants to encrypt message $m=3$ using Bob's public key $(n,e)$. Note that $n=77$, $e=7$. Use the repeated squaring technique to calculate the ciphertext $c=m^e$.
independentVerification: 3^2 mod77=9 and3^4 mod77=4;7=4+2+1;4*9*3 mod77=31. Original prompt omits modulus after m^e; named RSA context and official solution specify77. Wording retained.
officialMarkdown:
Source: [physical PDF page 12](../sources/papers/COMP2711_F2025_Final.pdf#page=12).

(iii) Encrypt message $m=3$ using Bob's public key $(n=77,e=7)$ by repeated squaring to compute $c=3^7\bmod77$.
$$\begin{aligned}3^1&\equiv3\pmod{77}\\3^2&\equiv9\pmod{77}\\3^4=(3^2)^2&\equiv9^2=81\equiv4\pmod{77}.\end{aligned}$$
Thus, the ciphertext is $3^7=3\times3^2\times3^4\pmod{77}=3\times9\times4\pmod{77}=31$.
$$c=31.$$
solutionMarkdown:
**Answer.** The RSA ciphertext is $c=31$.

**Derivation/proof.** RSA encryption uses the standard residue $c\equiv m^e\pmod n$. Modulo 77, $3^1\equiv3$, $3^2\equiv9$ and $3^4\equiv9^2=81\equiv4$. Since $7=4+2+1$,
$$3^7\equiv3^4\cdot3^2\cdot3\equiv4\cdot9\cdot3=108\equiv31\pmod{77}.$$
The value 31 lies between 0 and 76, so it is the ciphertext representative. Two squarings followed by multiplication implement the requested repeated-squaring method.
reviewMarkdown: The printed prompt ends with $c=m^e$ without writing the modulus. The RSA context and the official solution specify $c=m^e\bmod77$; the original prompt is retained.

questionMarkdown:
Prove the following equality without using repeated squaring:
$$46^{120}\bmod77=1.$$
[Hint: Make use of the fact that $77=11\cdot7$ and try to use Fermat's Little Theorem and the Chinese Reminder Theorem.]
independentVerification: 7 and11 prime;46 nonzero mod both;120 multiple of6 and10. FLT gives1 modulo7,11;CRT unique standard representative modulo77 is1. Direct pow confirms. Printed solution uses4 in second modulus where46 mod11=2; conclusion remains1, correct derivation preserved in supplement and separate review note.
officialMarkdown:
Source: [PDF physical page 7](../sources/papers/2013-final.pdf#page=7).

Let $r=46^{120}\bmod77$. Using Problem 1 (a), we get
$$r\bmod7=46^{120}\bmod7,r\bmod11=46^{120}\bmod11.$$
By Fermat's Little Theorem, we have
$$\begin{aligned}
46^{120}\bmod7&=(4^6)^{20}\bmod7=(4^6\bmod7)^{20}\bmod7=1,\\
46^{120}\bmod11&=(4^{10})^{12}\bmod11=(4^{10}\bmod11)^{12}\bmod11=1.
\end{aligned}$$
So, we have
$$r\bmod7=1,r\bmod11=1.$$
Obviously, we also have
$$1\bmod7=1,1\bmod11=1.$$
It follows from the Chinese Reminder Theorem that $r=1$. The proof is completed.
solutionMarkdown:
**Answer.** $46^{120}\equiv1\pmod{77}$.

**Derivation/proof.** Let $r=46^{120}\bmod77$. Since $77=7\cdot11$, Fermat gives $46^{120}=(46^6)^{20}\equiv1\pmod7$ and $46^{120}=(46^{10})^{12}\equiv1\pmod{11}$. The residue $1$ has the same two remainders, so CRT uniqueness yields $r=1$ modulo $77$.

Here $46\equiv4\pmod7$ and $46\equiv2\pmod{11}$, so both relevant bases are nonzero.
reviewMarkdown: The printed solution uses $4$ as the reduced base in the modulo-$11$ line, although $46\bmod11=2$. Its final answer is still correct. Use $46^{120}=(46^{10})^{12}\equiv1\pmod{11}$ (or use base $2$), together with the modulo-$7$ result. The Official Answer is preserved verbatim; the Supplementary Explanation gives the correct argument.

questionMarkdown: Show that $p^{q-1}+q^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod{pq}$ for any two distinct prime numbers $p$ and $q$.
independentVerification: For distinct primes p,q, p nonzero modq and q nonzero modp. FLT term gives1 and other positive-power term0 separately. Coprime divisibility gives1 modpq, including prime2. Enumerated all distinct primes<=199 as numerical cross-check.
officialMarkdown:
Source: [physical PDF page 3](../sources/papers/2021-midterm.pdf#page=3).

> By Fermat's little theorem, $p^{q-1}\equiv1\pmod q$.
> Clearly, $q^{p-1}\equiv0\pmod q$.
> Therefore, $p^{q-1}+q^{p-1}\equiv1+0\equiv1\pmod q$.
> Similarly, $p^{q-1}+q^{p-1}\equiv0+1\equiv1\pmod p$.
> By the Chinese remainder theorem, we have $p^{q-1}+q^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod{pq}$.
solutionMarkdown:
**Answer.** The congruence holds.

**Derivation/proof.** Modulo q, p is nonzero because the primes are distinct, so Fermat gives $p^{q-1}\equiv1$. Also $q^{p-1}\equiv0$ since p−1≥1. Their sum is 1 modulo q. Similarly it is 1 modulo p. Thus p and q both divide the sum minus one; because they are coprime, pq divides it. This proves the desired congruence, including the case where one prime is 2.

With $A=p^{q-1}+q^{p-1}$, the separate congruences give $q\mid A-1$ and $p\mid A-1$; coprimality gives $pq\mid A-1$.

questionMarkdown:
(a) Use Fermat’s Little Theorem and the Chinese Remainder Theorem to show that, if an integer $a$ is not divisible by any of 3, 5 and 7, then
$$a^{49}\bmod105=a\bmod105.$$
independentVerification: 48 divisible by2,4,6;given a nonzero modulo3,5,7. Thus a^49=a modulo each;CRT gives equal standard residues modulo105. Independently enumerated all a in0..104 with gcd(a,105)=1.
officialMarkdown:
Source: [PDF physical page 13](../sources/papers/2015-final.pdf#page=13).

(a) Note that $105=3\times5\times7$. We also have:
$$\begin{aligned}
a^{49}\bmod3&=(a^{24*(3-1)+1})\bmod3=a\bmod3&&\text{by FLT}\\
a^{49}\bmod5&=(a^{12*(5-1)+1})\bmod5=a\bmod5&&\text{by FLT}\\
a^{49}\bmod7&=(a^{8*(7-1)+1})\bmod7=a\bmod7&&\text{by FLT}
\end{aligned}$$
By CRT, we have
$$a^{49}\bmod3\times5=a\bmod15.$$
Applying CRT again we get
$$a^{49}\bmod15\times7=a\bmod105.$$
solutionMarkdown:
**Answer.** $a^{49}\equiv a\pmod{105}$.

**Derivation/proof.** For $r=3,5,7$, the hypothesis gives $\gcd(a,r)=1$, so $a^{r-1}\equiv1\pmod r$. Since $48=24\cdot2=12\cdot4=8\cdot6$, $a^{49}=a(a^{r-1})^{48/(r-1)}\equiv a\pmod r$. The pairwise coprime moduli multiply to 105; CRT therefore makes the two residues equal modulo 105.

CRT uniqueness makes the two standard remainders equal modulo the product $105$.
